newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Violence raises tensions in divided Bosnian town.
newsitem.headline: Violence raises tensions in divided Bosnian town.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem leaders on Friday appealed for calm in the divided Bosnian town of Mostar a day after seven explosions rocked the town centre.

The deputy mayor of Mostar, Safet Orucevic, and the president of the city council, Hamdija Jahic, issued a statement after international police monitors reported rifle grenades were fired at an apartment building on Thursday.

The incidents were orchestrated "by the same extremists who for more than three years have been intentionally terrorising the city and spreading hate in order to prevent any attempt to build co-existence", they said a statement.
The Bosnian state radio quoted the two leaders as urging citizens to allow reason to prevail and ignore "provocations".
Orucevic and Jahic called the violence a "reaction" by extremists who are threatened by peacetime negotiations aimed at ending the town's division into Croat and Moslem sectors.
Croat media, controlled by local Croat authorities, had quickly blamed Moslems in eastern Mostar for the explosions.

International police monitors reported two rifle grenades were fired at an apartment building in the Croat-held western part of Mostar and five other explosions were reported along a former front line on Thursday evening.
A spokesman for the U.N. police monitors said one of the rifle grenades hit the upper floor of an apartment building, tearing a hole in the wall of a flat.
The occupants of the flat were inside when the grenade hit but they survived without serious injury, said spokesman Frank Sarver.
The source of the other explosions was unclear and police monitors were still investigating, Sarver said by telephone.
International police monitors were concerned over the incidents and planned to step up patrols to try TO discourage further violence, he said.
Croats and Moslems, who began the Bosnian conflict as allies against Serb forces, waged a vicious 10-month war for territory that ended in 1994 under U.S. pressure.
Their fighting devastated Mostar and left the town divided into Moslem and Croat sectors.
This week's violence -- the worst in months -coincided with fierce political disputes between rival Croat and Moslem leaders in Mostar and elsewhere.
"When we have (political) tensions you have people who want to add fuel to the fire," said Dragan Gasic, spokesman for the Mostar office of the international High Representative to Bosnia.
The newly-elected municipal government charged with reunifying Mostar has no offices because Croat nationalists have occupied the building which was supposed to house the new administration.
A meeting of the cantonal government for the Mostar region ended in bitter disagreement on Thursday, with Moslem and Croat representatives unable to agree on a budget.
